title: Conversation Fillers and Listening Signals
goal: Give yourself thinking time, organize a turn, and show how you are following another person's story.

study.title: Small words can do different jobs

runs.text: A conversation does not have to run without pauses. Small words can help organize it, but adding one to every sentence is not the goal. Some so-called fillers communicate a real attitude or change of direction.

rows.text: Begin a thoughtful or qualified answer
Well, I liked the ending, but the beginning was slow.
Move to a topic or next step
So, what should we do next?
Acknowledge something or begin an action
It was expensive. I mean, more than I expected.
Actually, the meeting is on Thursday.
The movie was okay, I guess.

runs.text: These are examples of functions, not permanent translations.
Okay
can acknowledge information without enthusiastic agreement.
Actually
can correct someone; consider how the correction fits the relationship.
Making a choice
Did you enjoy the concert?

turns.speaker: Lee

runs.text: Well, the music was great. The room was just too crowded.

turns.en: Well, the music was great. The room was just too crowded.

runs.text: Oh, right.

turns.speaker: Lee

blocks.caption: Small words can do different jobs · Ari & Lee

runs.text: Lee does not simply answer yes or no. The small expressions help connect the positive and negative parts.

study.title: Casual speech and shades of meaning

runs.text: Kind of
can make an evaluation less definite:
I kind of liked it
To be honest
signals that you are presenting a candid view:
I'm too tired to go, to be honest
. Neither automatically makes the following comment gentle.
Informal
like
has several uses.
It took, like, twenty minutes
gives an approximate amount.
I was like, “Are we at the right place?”
presents a reaction, thought or reported words; it need not be an exact quotation. You can try these in an informal story. You do not have to copy them to make every sentence sound American.
You know
can appeal to something you expect the listener to understand:
It was one of those days, you know?
The listener may still need an explanation.

rows.text: A positive reaction to an activity.

turns.speaker: Lee

runs.text: We took the train to the coast.

turns.en: We took the train to the coast.

runs.text: Uh-huh.

turns.speaker: Lee

runs.text: But we got off at the wrong station.

turns.en: But we got off at the wrong station.

runs.text: Oh no! What happened next?

turns.speaker: Lee

turns.en: We walked to the beach. It was only ten minutes away.

runs.text: Oh, that's good.

blocks.caption: Show you are listening · Lee & Ari

runs.text: Following a story is different from agreeing with an opinion.
Uh-huh
alone does not tell Lee whether Ari approves of the decision.
A
tag question
adds a short question to a statement. Start with these complete patterns:
The class starts at six, doesn't it? — Yes, it does. / No, it starts at seven.
You're coming tomorrow, aren't you? — Yes, I am. / No, I can't.
You haven't seen my bag, have you? — No, I haven't. / Yes, it's by the door.
Use the reply to give the actual information. You can also ask a full question such as
Does the class start at six?
if the tag feels difficult.
Practice alone by speaking the story and then each response. With a partner, change roles.
Ari asks whether you liked a movie. Your role liked the acting but found the story confusing. Begin with
Well
and give both parts. Useful words:
The acting was good. The story was confusing.
Add one listening response after each event:
We won two tickets. / Then we missed the bus. / A friend gave us a ride.
Choose a reaction that fits each event.
Correct this detail:
The class is on Friday.
Your information says Thursday. Start with
Actually
and supply the correct day.
Someone asks
You're coming tomorrow, aren't you?
You cannot come. Answer and give the true information.
Hide the models. Tell a three-sentence story about a concert or trip. Add one thinking or organizing expression only where it serves a purpose. Then respond as the listener.
Sample possibilities
Well, the acting was good, but the story was confusing.
Wow! / Oh no! / Oh, that's good.
Actually, the class is on Thursday.
No, I can't.
Check:
Did your small words help the listener follow? Did the reactions fit the events? Could you give the correct information even when a question suggested a different answer?
